::: {#sol-deep-grad-norms}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
def deep_mlp(activation, n_hidden=10, width=32):
    _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
    layers, n_in = [], 64
    for layer in range(n_hidden):
        layers += [nn.Linear(n_in, width), activation()]
        n_in = width
    layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 10))
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)


grad_norms = {}
for name, activation in [("logistic", nn.Sigmoid), ("ReLU", nn.ReLU)]:
    net = deep_mlp(activation)
    loss_fn(net(x_train), y_train).backward()
    grad_norms[name] = [m.weight.grad.norm().item() for m in net if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for name, norms in grad_norms.items():
    ax.semilogy(range(1, len(norms) + 1), norms, marker="o", label=name)
ax.set_xlabel("layer (1 = first)")
ax.set_ylabel("size of weight gradient")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
shrink = {name: norms[-1] / norms[0] for name, norms in grad_norms.items()}
print(shrink)
```

The size is the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of the squared entries.
In both networks the gradient is largest at the last layer and smaller at each earlier layer.
With the logistic function,
the last layer's weight gradient is `r sprintf("%.0e", py$shrink[["logistic"]])` times the first layer's;
with the ReLU it is `r sprintf("%.0f", py$shrink[["ReLU"]])` times.
A training step with one learning rate would move the logistic network's first layers almost not at all.

:::
